claim: Cell division in Escherichia coli relies on the Z ring, a cytoskeletal structure that acts as a scaffold for the assembly of the divisome.
source: Cell division in Escherichia coli relies on the Z ring, a cytoskeletal structure that acts as a scaffold for the assembly of the divisome.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about bacterial cell division.

claim: At equimolar concentrations of ZapD and FtsZ, ZapD induces the formation of toroidal structures composed of short, curved FtsZ filaments that are crosslinked vertically, but also laterally and diagonally.
source: Using cryo-electron tomography and biochemical analysis, we show that, at equimolar concentrations of ZapD and FtsZ, ZapD induces the formation of toroidal structures composed of short, curved FtsZ filaments that are crosslinked vertically, but also laterally and diagonally.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-ET and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At higher concentrations of ZapD, regularly spaced ZapD dimers crosslink FtsZ filaments from above, resulting in the formation of straight bundles.
source: At higher concentrations of ZapD, regularly spaced ZapD dimers crosslink FtsZ filaments from above, resulting in the formation of straight bundles.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-ET observations and measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optimal crosslinking density and geometry play a key role in enabling filament curvature and ring formation.
source: These findings provide valuable insights into the structural organization and stabilization of the Z ring by Zap proteins in bacterial cells, revealing the key role of optimal crosslinking density and geometry in enabling filament curvature and ring formation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing different structures at different ZapD concentrations.

claim: FtsZ is a tubulin homolog that polymerizes in the presence of GTP beneath the inner membrane at the future division site.
source: At the core of this process in most bacteria is FtsZ, a tubulin homolog that polymerizes in the presence of GTP beneath the inner membrane at the future division site, providing a scaffold for recruiting other division proteins (Nogales et al., 1998; de Boer et al., 1992; Addinall and Lutkenhaus, 1996; McQuillen and Xiao, 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: FtsZ undergoes treadmilling due to polymerization-dependent GTP hydrolysis.
source: FtsZ undergoes treadmilling due to polymerization-dependent GTP hydrolysis, allowing the ring to exhibit its dynamic behavior (Wagstaff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: FtsZ filaments can assemble into various structures, including bundles, sheets, and toroids, depending on environmental conditions.
source: Depending on environmental conditions, FtsZ filaments can assemble into various structures, including bundles, sheets, and toroids (Lu et al., 2000; Mukherjee and Lutkenhaus, 1999; Löwe and Amos, 1999; González et al., 2003; Popp et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Membrane-tethered FtsZ assemblies are arranged as loosely structured spirals in the midcell region, guided by spatial regulators.
source: Membrane-tethered FtsZ assemblies are arranged as loosely structured spirals in the midcell region, guided by spatial regulators. These structures eventually coalesce to form a cohesive Z ring (Squyres et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Escherichia coli, FtsA and ZipA tether FtsZ to the membrane.
source: In Escherichia coli, FtsA and ZipA tether FtsZ to the membrane (Ma and Margolin, 1999; Hale and Boer, 2002; Wang et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FtsA, ZipA, and Zap proteins stabilize the Z ring.
source: In Escherichia coli, FtsA and ZipA tether FtsZ to the membrane (Ma and Margolin, 1999; Hale and Boer, 2002; Wang et al., 1997) and, together with a set of FtsZ-associated proteins (Zaps), stabilize the ring (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2013; Durand-Heredia et al., 2011; Ebersbach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Min proteins inhibit FtsZ assembly at the polar regions.
source: Conversely, negative modulators inhibit FtsZ assembly at other sites, namely Min proteins at the polar regions (de Boer et al., 1989)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SlmA inhibits FtsZ assembly on the nucleoid.
source: Conversely, negative modulators inhibit FtsZ assembly at other sites, namely Min proteins at the polar regions (de Boer et al., 1989) and SlmA on the nucleoid (Tonthat et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most FtsZ modulators interact with FtsZ through its carboxy-terminal end (CCTP).
source: Most of these modulators interact with FtsZ through its carboxy-terminal end (CCTP), which modulates division assembly as a central hub (Ortiz et al., 2016; Buske and Levin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ZapD is the only Zap protein known to crosslink FtsZ by binding CCTP.
source: ZapD is the only Zap protein known to crosslink FtsZ by binding CCTP, suggesting a critical Z ring structure stabilizing function (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012; Schumacher et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2016; Roach et al., 2016; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Zap proteins play overlapping roles in stabilizing the Z ring during cell division.
source: Zap proteins play overlapping roles in stabilizing the Z ring during cell division.
evidence: This is a general statement about Zap protein function supported by the literature.

claim: Zap proteins are nonessential for division, but their absence leads to less compact Z rings.
source: Although they are nonessential for division, their absence leads to less compact Z rings, and the knowout of two or more Zap encoding genes simultaneously results in cell elongation (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012; Buss et al., 2013; Hale et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The knockout of two or more Zap encoding genes simultaneously results in cell elongation.
source: Although they are nonessential for division, their absence leads to less compact Z rings, and the knowout of two or more Zap encoding genes simultaneously results in cell elongation (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012; Buss et al., 2013; Hale et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different Zap proteins do not share any sequence homology and differ in their structure and filament crosslinking mechanism.
source: Notably, these different Zap proteins do not share any sequence homology and differ in their structure and filament crosslinking mechanism (Huang et al., 2013; Schumacher et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Zap proteins may actively remove FtsZ from the septum during the final stages of constriction.
source: Additionally, Zap proteins may actively remove FtsZ from the septum during the final stages of constriction (Pazos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Zap proteins facilitate the positioning of the Z ring at the replication terminus of the chromosome by interacting with MatP.
source: They also facilitate the positioning of the Z ring at the replication terminus of the chromosome by interacting with MatP, which forms a scaffolding anchor known as Ter-linkage (Bailey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ZapD is a symmetrical dimer consisting of an α-helical domain and a β-sheet domain containing a positively charged binding pocket required for crosslinking and bundling FtsZ filaments.
source: ZapD is a symmetrical dimer consisting of an α-helical domain and a β-sheet domain containing a positively charged binding pocket required for crosslinking and bundling FtsZ filaments (Roach et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: ZapD binds to the CCTP of FtsZ through electrostatic interactions.
source: ZapD binds to the CCTP of FtsZ through electrostatic interactions (Roach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ZapD crosslinks FtsZ filaments, promoting bundling and significantly reducing the GTPase activity of FtsZ.
source: ZapD crosslinks FtsZ filaments, promoting bundling and significantly reducing the GTPase activity of FtsZ (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A model of how ZapD crosslinks neighboring FtsZ filaments has been proposed based on the structural analysis of ZapD-FtsZ interactions.
source: A model of how ZapD crosslinks neighboring FtsZ filaments has been proposed based on the structural analysis of ZapD-FtsZ interactions (Schumacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the proposed model, the ZapD dimer connects two FtsZ filaments through the CCTP, which could organize them in a parallel or antiparallel orientation due to the flexibility provided by the flexible linker.
source: In this model, the ZapD dimer connects two FtsZ filaments through the CCTP, which could organize them in a parallel or antiparallel orientation due to the flexibility provided by the flexible linker (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on a prior model and referenced in Figure 1a.

claim: The experimental validation of the ZapD crosslinking model is still missing.
source: However, the experimental validation of this model is still missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The link between FtsZ bundling promoted by ZapD and the large-scale organization of FtsZ filaments remains unresolved.
source: Furthermore, the link between FtsZ bundling, promoted by ZapD, and the large-scale organization of FtsZ filaments remains unresolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: FtsZ crosslinking proteins collectively play a critical role in the condensation and stability of the Z ring in different organisms.
source: Recently, Gong et al., 2024, demonstrated that although the FtsZ crosslinking proteins are not individually essential, they collectively play a critical role in the condensation and stability of the Z ring in different organisms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: The specific mechanisms driving Z ring condensation remain unclear.
source: However, the specific mechanisms driving this condensation remain unclear, highlighting the complexity of the bacterial cell division process.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge.

claim: ZapD forms stable dimers.
source: First, we confirmed that ZapD forms stable dimers, which is consistent with previous studies (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1aI and b).
evidence: This is supported by AUC data presented in the manuscript and citations to prior work.

claim: Unpolymerized FtsZ-GDP primarily self-assembles from monomers into dimers and other oligomeric species, albeit in small proportions.
source: In contrast, unpolymerized FtsZ-GDP primarily self-assembles from monomers into dimers and other oligomeric species, albeit in small proportions, as expected (Rivas et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 1aII).
evidence: This is supported by AUC data and a citation to prior work.

claim: Sedimentation velocity analysis of mixtures of ZapD and FtsZ revealed the presence of two predominant molecular species of ZapD:FtsZ complexes in solution, compatible with ZapD dimers bound to one or two FtsZ monomers.
source: Sedimentation velocity analysis of mixtures of the two proteins revealed the presence of two predominant molecular species of ZapD:FtsZ complexes in solution. These complexes are compatible with ZapD dimers bound to one or two FtsZ monomers, corresponding to ZapD:FtsZ stoichiometries of 2:1 and 1:1, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1aIII–IV).
evidence: This is supported by AUC data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The interaction between ZapD and FtsZ was confirmed using fluorescence anisotropy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed the interaction of both proteins using fluorescence anisotropy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When testing GTP-FtsZ filaments at 5 or 10 μM concentrations, negligible turbidity was found, similar to that of ZapD alone at concentrations ranging from 1 to 40 μM.
source: When testing GTP-FtsZ filaments at 5 or 10 μM concentrations, we found negligible turbidity, similar to that of ZapD alone at concentrations ranging from 1 to 40 μM.
evidence: This is supported by turbidity measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: When ZapD was added to FtsZ, the turbidity of the FtsZ polymers increased, reaching a maximum at approximately 5 μM of ZapD (with a ZapD-FtsZ molar ratio of around 1).
source: However, when ZapD was added, the turbidity of the FtsZ polymers increased, reaching a maximum at approximately 5 μM of ZapD (with a ZapD-FtsZ molar ratio of around 1). This turbidity level did not change significantly even at higher ZapD concentrations (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by turbidity measurements presented in Figure 1b.

claim: FtsZ bundles with ZapD exhibited reduced GTPase activity, reaching 20% at equimolar or higher concentrations of ZapD.
source: Compared to FtsZ filaments observed in vitro, FtsZ bundles with ZapD exhibited reduced GTPase activity, reaching 20% at equimolar or higher concentrations of ZapD (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), in agreement with previous studies (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by GTPase activity measurements presented in Figure 1c and a citation to prior work.

claim: The macrostructures formed by FtsZ in the presence of ZapD were disassembled more slowly than the FtsZ filaments upon GTP consumption.
source: The macrostructures formed by FtsZ in the presence of ZapD were disassembled more slowly than the FtsZ filaments upon GTP consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by turbidity measurements over time presented in the manuscript.

claim: Replenishment of GTP allowed for a partial recovery of the turbidity signal, suggesting that the FtsZ bundles can be rapidly reassembled.
source: Replenishment of GTP allowed for a partial recovery of the turbidity signal, suggesting that the FtsZ bundles can be rapidly reassembled (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: This is supported by turbidity measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: High concentrations of macromolecular crowders (such as Ficoll or dextran) promote the formation of dynamic FtsZ polymer networks.
source: Previous studies have shown that high concentrations of macromolecular crowders (such as Ficoll or dextran) promote the formation of dynamic FtsZ polymer networks (González et al., 2003), observations that are consistent with our results.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and comparison to current results.

claim: In the 5–10 μM ZapD concentration range, the bundles exhibited an estimated ZapD binding stoichiometry of approximately 0.3–0.4, meaning that one ZapD dimer is associated with every four to six FtsZ monomers.
source: Our results showed that in the 5–10 μM ZapD concentration range, the bundles exhibited an estimated ZapD binding stoichiometry of approximately 0.3–0.4, meaning that one ZapD dimer is associated with every four to six FtsZ monomers.
evidence: This is supported by analytical centrifugation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At higher ZapD concentrations (30–40 μM), the binding stoichiometry increased to 1.1±0.2, indicating one ZapD dimer for every two FtsZ monomers.
source: In contrast, at higher ZapD concentrations (30–40 μM), the binding stoichiometry increased to 1.1±0.2, indicating one ZapD dimer for every two FtsZ monomers.
evidence: This is supported by analytical centrifugation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ZapD binding stoichiometry in the polymers increases with higher ZapD concentrations.
source: These results suggest that the ZapD binding stoichiometry in the polymers increases with higher ZapD concentrations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analytical centrifugation data.

claim: In the presence of GTP, FtsZ polymerized into thin filaments of variable length and curvature.
source: In the presence of GTP, FtsZ polymerized into thin filaments of variable length and curvature (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM images presented in Figure 2a.

claim: Upon addition of equimolar amounts of ZapD, FtsZ filaments assembled into bundles that predominantly formed circular toroidal structures.
source: Upon addition of equimolar amounts of ZapD, corresponding to the slightly substoichiometric ZapD binding densities described in the previous section, FtsZ filaments assembled into bundles that predominantly formed circular toroidal structures (Figure 2b and c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), making them a compelling study target.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM images presented in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The toroidal structures have an outer diameter on the order of the bacterial cell size (502±55 nm).
source: Quantitative analysis of the toroidal structure revealed a conserved organization, with an outer diameter on the order of the bacterial cell size (502±55 nm) (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM images presented in Figure 2d.

claim: The toroidal structures have a typical thickness of 127±25 nm.
source: Quantitative analysis of the toroidal structure revealed a conserved organization, with an outer diameter on the order of the bacterial cell size (502±55 nm) (Figure 2d), a typical thickness of 127±25 nm (Figure 2e)
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM images presented in Figure 2e.

claim: The toroidal structures have an average height of 93±15 nm.
source: Quantitative analysis of the toroidal structure revealed a conserved organization, with an outer diameter on the order of the bacterial cell size (502±55 nm) (Figure 2d), a typical thickness of 127±25 nm (Figure 2e), and an average height of 93±15 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The circularity of the toroidal structure was 0.92±0.1 and 0.85±0.1 for the outer and inner diameters, respectively.
source: By measuring the shortest and longest axes, we determined that the circularity of the structure was 0.92±0.1 and 0.85±0.1 for the outer and inner diameters, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM images presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The conserved toroidal structure could result from the intrinsic curvature of the FtsZ filaments stabilized by ZapD binding.
source: This conserved toroidal structure could result from the intrinsic curvature of the FtsZ filaments (Lu et al., 2000; Huecas et al., 2017; Erickson and Osawa, 2017) stabilized by ZapD binding.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and citations to prior work on FtsZ curvature.

claim: The dimension of a ZapD dimer is ~7 nm along its longest axis.
source: The dimension of a ZapD dimer is ~7 nm along its longest axis.
evidence: This is a statement about the known structure of ZapD.

claim: Huecas et al., 2017, estimated an interfilament distance of ~6.5–6.7 nm for toroids of Bacillus subtilis FtsZ.
source: Huecas et al., 2017, estimated an interfilament distance of ~6.5–6.7 nm for toroids of Bacillus subtilis FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A similar spacing for double filaments (5.9±0.8 nm) was observed in the absence of ZapD.
source: We observed a similar spacing for double filaments (5.9±0.8 nm) and a longer spacing in the presence of ZapD (7.88±2.1 nm).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM/ET data.

claim: A longer spacing (7.88±2.1 nm) was observed in the presence of ZapD.
source: We observed a similar spacing for double filaments (5.9±0.8 nm) and a longer spacing in the presence of ZapD (7.88±2.1 nm).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM/ET data.

claim: Previous studies with ZapD have suggested that distances of 6–12 nm are possible based on the protein structure.
source: Previous studies with ZapD have suggested that distances of 6–12 nm are possible based on the protein structure (Schumacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ZapD dimers crosslink adjacent FtsZ filaments into bundles and toroids.
source: Our data showed that ZapD dimers crosslink adjacent FtsZ filaments into bundles and toroids.
evidence: This is a summary of the cryo-EM/ET data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The toroids are remarkably regular in size and similar to the bacterial diameter.
source: These toroids are remarkably regular in size and similar to the bacterial diameter (McQuillen and Xiao, 2020; Fu et al., 2010; Li et al., 2007), suggesting a conserved intrinsic curvature of the FtsZ filaments across a range of ZapD bonds (Erickson and Osawa, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM data and citations to prior work on bacterial cell size.

claim: Cryo-ET revealed the dense packing of the toroidal structures, with numerous densities connecting the FtsZ filaments laterally or diagonally.
source: Cryo-ET revealed the dense packing of the toroidal structures, with numerous densities connecting the FtsZ filaments laterally or diagonally (Figure 3a–c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Zoomed-in views of the toroids in the XY plane showed that the toroid consists of relatively short filament segments arranged nearly parallel or antiparallel to each other.
source: Zoomed-in views of the toroids in the XY plane showed that the toroid consists of relatively short filament segments arranged nearly parallel or antiparallel to each other (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: Cross-sectional views of the toroids revealed elongated structures rather than simple filament cross-sections along the Z-axis.
source: In contrast, cross-sectional views of the toroids revealed elongated structures rather than simple filament cross-sections along the Z-axis (Figure 3c, left, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 3c.

claim: The isosurface confirmed the presence of extended structures along the Z-axis, well beyond the elongation expected from the missing wedge effect for single FtsZ filaments.
source: The isosurface confirmed the presence of extended structures along the Z-axis, well beyond the elongation expected from the missing wedge effect for single FtsZ filaments (for comparison, see Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and comparison to control filaments.

claim: The vertically extended structures appeared to correspond to filaments that were connected or decorated by additional densities along the Z-axis.
source: The vertically extended structures appeared to correspond to filaments that were connected or decorated by additional densities along the Z-axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: These densities were only observed in the presence of ZapD, suggesting that they represent ZapD connections.
source: Importantly, these densities were only observed in the presence of ZapD (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b), suggesting that they represent ZapD connections (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplements 2e and 3b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of cryo-ET data with and without ZapD.

claim: The toroids are constructed and stabilized by interactions between ZapD and FtsZ, which are mainly formed along the Z-axis but also vertically and diagonally.
source: These results suggest that the toroids are constructed and stabilized by interactions between ZapD and FtsZ, which are mainly formed along the Z-axis but also vertically and diagonally.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data.

claim: Most connections exhibited a characteristic bi-spherical shape between the filaments, reminiscent of ZapD dimers.
source: Most connections exhibited a characteristic bi-spherical shape between the filaments, reminiscent of ZapD dimers (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Lateral connections between two parallel FtsZ filaments at the same height within the toroid were observed.
source: We observed lateral connections between two parallel FtsZ filaments at the same height within the toroid (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 4b.

claim: FtsZ filaments at different heights can connect vertically and diagonally through ZapD proteins acting as bridging units, forming a complex 3D mesh.
source: In addition, FtsZ filaments at different heights can connect vertically and diagonally through ZapD proteins acting as bridging units, forming a complex 3D mesh (Figure 4c and d and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Potential ZapD proteins that decorate individual FtsZ filaments and can link them to other nearby filaments were identified.
source: We also identified potential ZapD proteins that decorate individual FtsZ filaments and can link them to other nearby filaments (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 4b.

claim: Some filaments exhibited multiple crosslinks, leading to stronger attachments between them.
source: Furthermore, some filaments exhibited multiple crosslinks, leading to stronger attachments between them (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 4d.

claim: The short filament length, which results in gaps between adjacent filaments, does not correlate with a higher number of ZapD connections.
source: The short filament length, which results in gaps between adjacent filaments, does not correlate with a higher number of ZapD connections (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that ZapD is able to crosslink filaments in all directions without causing filament breakage.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of cryo-ET data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At high concentrations of ZapD (typically 40–60 μM, representing a molar ratio of approximately one to four or six to FtsZ), the formation of straight bundles with striated patterns between the FtsZ filaments was observed.
source: At high concentrations of ZapD (typically 40–60 μM, representing a molar ratio of approximately one to four or six to FtsZ), we observed the formation of straight bundles with striated patterns between the FtsZ filaments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), as well as the presence of some toroidal structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The high concentration of ZapD molecules increased the number of links between the filaments and ultimately promoted the formation of straight bundles.
source: Here, the high concentration of ZapD molecules increased the number of links between the filaments and ultimately promoted the formation of straight bundles, indicating that the assembly of FtsZ-ZapD structures is a reversible process that strongly depends on the amount of ZapD proteins crosslinking the filaments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The assembly of FtsZ-ZapD structures is a reversible process that strongly depends on the amount of ZapD proteins crosslinking the filaments.
source: Here, the high concentration of ZapD molecules increased the number of links between the filaments and ultimately promoted the formation of straight bundles, indicating that the assembly of FtsZ-ZapD structures is a reversible process that strongly depends on the amount of ZapD proteins crosslinking the filaments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data.

claim: Toroids and curved bundles always coexist, but the predominance shifts from toroids to straight bundles at high ZapD concentrations.
source: Toroids and curved bundles always coexist, but the predominance shifts from toroids to straight bundles at high ZapD concentrations.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The number of crosslinks between filaments can modulate the properties of the assembled higher-order structures, resulting in the reorganization of the toroidal structures into straight bundles upon ZapD saturation.
source: This shift suggests that the number of crosslinks between filaments can modulate the properties of the assembled higher-order structures, resulting in the reorganization of the toroidal structures into straight bundles upon ZapD saturation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The straight bundles consist of a highly organized stack of well-aligned FtsZ filaments.
source: The straight bundles are formed at high ZapD concentrations and consist of a highly organized stack of well-aligned FtsZ filaments (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: The connection of filaments by multiple putative ZapD proteins results in the straightening of the structure of the filaments.
source: The connection of filaments by multiple putative ZapD proteins results in the straightening of the structure of the filaments (Lu et al., 2000; Erickson and Osawa, 2017; Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and citations to prior work.

claim: ZapD crosslinks FtsZ filaments vertically, forming a row of ZapD proteins interacting with both filaments.
source: Interestingly, ZapD crosslinks FtsZ filaments vertically, forming a row of ZapD proteins interacting with both filaments (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data presented in Figure 5d.

claim: The distance between ZapD proteins in straight bundles provided a mean value of 4.5±0.5 nm.
source: The distance between ZapD proteins provided a mean value of 4.5±0.5 nm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a), consistent with the size of FtsZ proteins (Huecas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data and a citation to prior work.

claim: Most FtsZ proteins interact with the ZapD dimers that crosslink the filaments in straight bundles.
source: This observation suggests that most FtsZ proteins interact with the ZapD dimers that crosslink the filaments, in agreement with the ZapD enrichment in the bundles observed by sedimentation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the spacing measurements and sedimentation data.

claim: The presence of ZapD increased the distance between two FtsZ filaments connected by ZapD proteins compared with the spacing in the absence of ZapD.
source: In addition, we found that the presence of ZapD increased the distance between two FtsZ filaments connected by ZapD proteins compared with the spacing in the absence of ZapD, regardless of the amount of ZapD connections (from 5.9±0.8 to 7.88±2 nm in toroids and 7.6±1.5 nm in straight bundles; Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM/ET data.

claim: ZapD not only connects neighboring FtsZ filaments but spreads them apart.
source: This indicates that ZapD not only connects neighboring FtsZ filaments but spreads them apart, which could have important implications for the functionality of the Z ring.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spacing measurements.

claim: The bundles formed at high ZapD concentrations correspond to a binding saturation regime in which a ZapD dimer binds two FtsZ molecules connecting two filaments, straightening their structure and arranging them into large, highly organized straight bundles.
source: The bundles formed at the high ZapD concentrations tested (up to four molar excess of ZapD to FtsZ) correspond to a binding saturation regime in which a ZapD dimer binds two FtsZ molecules connecting two filaments, straightening their structure and arranging them into large, highly organized straight bundles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data and binding stoichiometry measurements.

claim: Fewer connections provide the freedom to form toroidal structures.
source: In contrast, fewer connections provide the freedom to form toroidal structures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data.

claim: A certain number of ZapD-driven bonds are optimal for maintaining the preferential curvature of FtsZ filaments and allowing toroid assembly.
source: This observation confirms that a certain number of ZapD-driven bonds are optimal for maintaining the preferential curvature of FtsZ filaments and allowing toroid assembly, establishing a structural dependence of assembled bundles on the number of ZapD-mediated bonds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data.

claim: Dimerization of ZapD is essential to promote the assembly of organized high-order FtsZ structures such as toroids and straight bundles.
source: These results demonstrated that dimerization of ZapD is essential to promote the assembly of organized high-order FtsZ structures such as toroids and straight bundles, highlighting the structural importance of stable ZapD-driven connections between filaments.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data with the mZapD mutant.

claim: ZapD crosslinks FtsZ in solution to form 3D toroidal structures characterized by short, discontinuous FtsZ filaments that are vertically stacked and crosslinked, as well as diagonally and laterally crosslinked.
source: Our results indicate that ZapD crosslinks FtsZ in solution to form 3D toroidal structures characterized by short, discontinuous FtsZ filaments that are vertically stacked and crosslinked, as well as diagonally and laterally crosslinked, as revealed by cryo-ET.
evidence: This is a summary of the cryo-ET data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The relative concentrations of FtsZ and ZapD dictate the assembly geometry.
source: The relative concentrations of FtsZ and ZapD dictate the assembly geometry.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the manuscript.

claim: FtsZ toroids emerge as the dominant structure when both proteins are present in equimolar ratios.
source: Remarkably, FtsZ toroids emerge as the dominant structure when both proteins are present in equimolar ratios, whereas straight bundles are assembled at high concentrations of ZapD.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the manuscript.

claim: Straight bundles are assembled at high concentrations of ZapD.
source: Remarkably, FtsZ toroids emerge as the dominant structure when both proteins are present in equimolar ratios, whereas straight bundles are assembled at high concentrations of ZapD.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the manuscript.

claim: The balance between vertical and lateral or diagonal crosslinking is important to allow for the filament curvature observed in the toroids.
source: Our study highlights the importance of the balance between vertical and lateral or diagonal crosslinking to allow for the filament curvature observed in the toroids, which is absent in the straight bundles where vertical crosslinking is dominant.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data.

claim: The observation of toroidal FtsZ structures promoted by ZapD in solution is consistent with the observation of pre-curved FtsZ protofilaments in circular assemblies attached to model membranes in various in vitro systems.
source: Our observation of toroidal FtsZ structures promoted by ZapD in solution is consistent with the observation of pre-curved FtsZ protofilaments in circular assemblies attached to model membranes in various in vitro systems (Loose and Mitchison, 2014; Ramirez-Diaz et al., 2018; Vélez, 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior work.

claim: FtsZ can form ring-shaped structures with diameters ranging from 100 to 200 nm on surfaces, becoming more pronounced when adsorbed to lipid, carbon, or mica surfaces.
source: Additionally, FtsZ can form ring-shaped structures with diameters ranging from 100 to 200 nm on surfaces, becoming more pronounced when adsorbed to lipid, carbon, or mica surfaces (Huecas et al., 2007; Mingorance et al., 2005; González et al., 2005), or in the presence of molecular crowders like methylcellulose (Popp et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cryo-EM of concentrated (50 μM) FtsZ from B. subtilis with GMPCPP revealed that these protofilaments often coalesce into spirals or toroids, forming large aggregates.
source: Cryo-EM of concentrated (50 μM) FtsZ from B. subtilis with GMPCPP revealed that these protofilaments often coalesce into spirals or toroids, forming large aggregates (Huecas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: These toroidal structures correspond to the curved conformations of FtsZ polymers observed in various bacterial species, which are thought to contribute to the generation of constriction forces.
source: These toroidal structures correspond to the curved conformations of FtsZ polymers observed in various bacterial species, which are thought to contribute to the generation of constriction forces (Erickson and Osawa, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In E. coli, approximately 5000 FtsZ monomers (about one third of the intracellular concentration of FtsZ) could circle the cell six to eight times.
source: In E. coli, approximately 5000 FtsZ monomers (about one third of the intracellular concentration of FtsZ) could circle the cell six to eight times (Stricker et al., 2002), suggesting a discontinuous toroidal assembly.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ZapD is present at approximately 500 molecules per cell.
source: ZapD, present at approximately 500 molecules per cell (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012), represents only a small fraction of the FtsZ molecules and favors the formation of toroidal structures in the absence of interactions with other FtsZ-associated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ZapD represents only a small fraction of the FtsZ molecules and favors the formation of toroidal structures in the absence of interactions with other FtsZ-associated proteins.
source: ZapD, present at approximately 500 molecules per cell (Durand-Heredia et al., 2012), represents only a small fraction of the FtsZ molecules and favors the formation of toroidal structures in the absence of interactions with other FtsZ-associated proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and known cellular concentrations.

claim: Higher concentrations of ZapD would be required to form straight bundles.
source: Higher concentrations of ZapD would be required to form straight bundles.

claim: The persistence length and curvature of FtsZ filaments are optimized to form bacterial-sized ring structures.
source: The persistence length and curvature of FtsZ filaments are optimized to form bacterial-sized ring structures (McQuillen and Xiao, 2020; Erickson and Osawa, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ZapD helps to stabilize toroids by crosslinking and increasing the spacing between FtsZ filaments from 5.9±0.8 to 7.9±2 nm in toroids and 7.6±1.5 nm in straight bundles.
source: ZapD helps to stabilize these toroids by crosslinking and increasing the spacing between FtsZ filaments from 5.9±0.8 to 7.9±2 nm in toroids and 7.6±1.5 nm in straight bundles (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryo-EM/ET data.

claim: The increased spacing promotes a more dynamic organization, providing functional flexibility in bacteria.
source: This increased spacing promotes a more dynamic organization, providing functional flexibility in bacteria.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spacing measurements.

claim: The linker connecting ZapD to FtsZ can also modulate filament spacing and curvature.
source: The linker connecting ZapD to FtsZ can also modulate filament spacing and curvature (Huecas et al., 2017; Sundararajan and Goley, 2017; Sundararajan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A mixture of curvatures in the internal organization of the toroids is observed.
source: We observe a mixture of curvatures in the internal organization of the toroids.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET data.

claim: While FtsZ filaments have a preferred curvature, the density of ZapD connections forces the structure to adapt and align with neighboring filaments, thereby affecting FtsZ curvature.
source: While FtsZ filaments have a preferred curvature, the density of ZapD connections forces the structure to adapt and align with neighboring filaments, thereby affecting FtsZ curvature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data.

claim: The assembly of functional, curved FtsZ macrostructures occurs only within a specific stoichiometric range of ZapD-FtsZ interactions.
source: We therefore hypothesize that the assembly of functional, curved FtsZ macrostructures occurs only within a specific stoichiometric range of ZapD-FtsZ interactions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data.

claim: An increase in crosslinking at higher ZapD concentrations appears to cause the FtsZ polymer to form rigid, straight bundles.
source: An increase in crosslinking at higher ZapD concentrations appears to cause the FtsZ polymer to form rigid, straight bundles (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data.

claim: Only a robust ZapD dimer can form FtsZ toroids and straight filaments, indicating that a certain binding strength is necessary to bundle the filaments and maintain their structure.
source: Additionally, only a robust ZapD dimer can form FtsZ toroids and straight filaments, indicating that a certain binding strength is necessary to bundle the filaments and maintain their structure.

claim: ZapD can modulate the behavior of the entire structure through a concentration-dependent mechanism.
source: These observations, along with the high conformational variability found in ZapD connections, suggest that ZapD can modulate the behavior of the entire structure through a concentration-dependent mechanism.

claim: This structural reorganization highlights the polymorphic nature of the assemblies formed by FtsZ.
source: This structural reorganization highlights the polymorphic nature of the assemblies formed by FtsZ (Mateos-Gil et al., 2019; Monterroso et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data and citations to prior work.

claim: ZapD-mediated FtsZ toroids replicate some of the structural features of the Z ring architecture observed in vivo.
source: We also demonstrated that ZapD-mediated FtsZ toroids replicate some of the structural features of the Z ring architecture observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to in vivo observations.

claim: The current model of the Z ring describes a somewhat discontinuous and heterogeneous structure composed of randomly overlapping filaments.
source: Based on super-resolution imaging and cryo-ET, the current model of the Z ring describes a somewhat discontinuous and heterogeneous structure composed of randomly overlapping filaments (Szwedziak et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2010; Rowlett and Margolin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: These filaments arrange into a belt-like macromolecular entity, containing nodes with a higher density of dispersed filaments confined to a toroidal zone approximately 80–100 nm wide (toroidal height) and about 40–60 nm thick, located 13–16 nm below the inner membrane.
source: These filaments arrange into a belt-like macromolecular entity, containing nodes with a higher density of dispersed filaments confined to a toroidal zone approximately 80–100 nm wide (toroidal height) and about 40–60 nm thick, located 13–16 nm below the inner membrane (Szwedziak et al., 2014; Buss et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2010; Lyu et al., 2016; Rowlett and Margolin, 2014; Holden et al., 2014; Szwedziak and Ghosal, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The toroidal structures promoted by ZapD exhibit dimensions within the range of the Z ring observed in vivo.
source: The toroidal structures promoted by ZapD exhibit dimensions within this range.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to in vivo observations.

claim: The thickness and multilayering of the toroids are significantly greater than the Z ring, likely due to the absence of other cellular components competing for binding with FtsZ.
source: However, their thickness and multilayering are significantly greater, likely due to the absence of other cellular components competing for binding with FtsZ.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: The Z ring model suggests that FtsZ filaments are weakly associated with one another through protein factors such as Zaps and weak FtsZ-FtsZ interactions, which may be crucial for their functionality.
source: The Z ring model also suggests that FtsZ filaments are weakly associated with one another through protein factors such as Zaps and weak FtsZ-FtsZ interactions, which may be crucial for their functionality (McQuillen and Xiao, 2020; Huecas et al., 2017; Sundararajan and Goley, 2017; Haeusser et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: One of the Zap proteins can stabilize and enhance associations between neighboring FtsZ filaments.
source: Our findings indicate that one of the Zap proteins can stabilize and enhance associations between neighboring FtsZ filaments.

claim: The intrinsic features of the toroidal structures share commonalities with the bacterial division ring.
source: We believe that the intrinsic features of the toroidal structures share commonalities with the bacterial division ring.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: The structures observed following ZapD crosslinking of FtsZ filaments may reveal inherent features that occur in vivo.
source: Despite the differences and limitations that may arise from an in vitro approach, the structures observed following ZapD crosslinking of FtsZ filaments may reveal inherent features that occur in vivo.

claim: The current model of the division ring consists of an array of filaments loosely connected by crosslinkers at the center of the cell, forming a ring.
source: The current model of the division ring consists of an array of filaments loosely connected by crosslinkers at the center of the cell, forming a ring.

claim: The binding of ZapA to FtsZ in equimolar mixtures induces the effective alignment and straightening of FtsZ filaments tethered to lipid bilayers by FtsA protein.
source: The binding of ZapA, a key member of the FtsZ-associated proteins family, to FtsZ in equimolar mixtures induces the effective alignment and straightening of FtsZ filaments tethered to lipid bilayers by FtsA protein, as demonstrated through high-resolution fluorescence microscopy and precise quantitative image analysis (Caldas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The interaction between ZapA and FtsZ reveals a structure comprising one ZapA tetramer for every four FtsZ molecules in the polymer.
source: This interaction reveals a structure comprising one ZapA tetramer for every four FtsZ molecules in the polymer, highlighting the organized nature of these interactions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The straight, parallel polymers manifested when ZapA occupies all binding sites bear striking resemblance to the straight bundles identified in this study at high concentrations of ZapD, indicative of binding saturation.
source: It is noteworthy that these straight, parallel polymers – manifested when ZapA occupies all binding sites – bear striking resemblance to the straight bundles identified in this study at high concentrations of ZapD, indicative of binding saturation.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior work on ZapA.

claim: FtsA and ZipA have a greater affinity for the CCTP of FtsZ than ZapD.
source: It is important to note that FtsA and ZipA have a greater affinity for the CCTP of FtsZ than ZapD.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative affinities of different FtsZ-binding proteins.

claim: Cryo-ET data on straight bundles provide new perspectives on how ZapD-FtsZ structures can effectively bind to the plasma membrane.
source: Our cryo-ET data on straight bundles provide new perspectives on how ZapD-FtsZ structures can effectively bind to the plasma membrane; in particular, the CCTP of parallel FtsZ filaments is oriented upward, allowing direct membrane binding or interaction with ZapDs that reinforce these filaments from above, rather than from the side, as previously suggested (Schumacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data and comparison to a prior model.

claim: The CCTP of parallel FtsZ filaments in straight bundles is oriented upward, allowing direct membrane binding or interaction with ZapDs that reinforce these filaments from above.
source: Our cryo-ET data on straight bundles provide new perspectives on how ZapD-FtsZ structures can effectively bind to the plasma membrane; in particular, the CCTP of parallel FtsZ filaments is oriented upward, allowing direct membrane binding or interaction with ZapDs that reinforce these filaments from above, rather than from the side, as previously suggested (Schumacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-ET data.

claim: The revelation that ring morphology depends on the binding stoichiometry between FtsZ and the crosslinking ZapD is invaluable.
source: The revelation that ring morphology depends on the binding stoichiometry between FtsZ and the crosslinking ZapD is invaluable, particularly as we integrate this knowledge into current reconstitution assays in membrane systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: There are alternative mechanisms for filament remodeling that do not rely on molecular motors, instead harnessing entropic forces via diffusible crosslinkers.
source: Although conventional wisdom points to molecular motors as the primary drivers of filament remodeling through energy consumption, there is increasing evidence that there are alternative mechanisms that do not rely on such energy, instead harnessing entropic forces via diffusible crosslinkers (Braun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: This approach may also be applicable to ZapD and FtsZ polymers.
source: This approach may also be applicable to ZapD and FtsZ polymers, suggesting a promising avenue for optimizing conditions in the reverse engineering of the division ring to enhance force generation in minimally reconstituted systems aimed at achieving autonomous cell division.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the findings.
